checks.claim: Saturated soil typically weighs roughly 100 to 130 pounds per cubic foot, depending on soil type (saturated clay is about 130 lb/ft3).
checks.why: Saturated clay is listed at 130 lb/ft3, but a topsoil supplier gives saturated topsoil at 96-111 lb/ft3, so 'over 100' is not true for all soils. The notes suggest 'roughly 100 to 130 lb/ft3 for most saturated soils'. Support comes from commercial pages, and the textbook excerpt did not show the values.

sources.title: What Is 1 cu ft soil weight? A Practical Guide
Cubic Yard of Topsoil Weight: 1,500-3,000 lbs Explained

checks.claim: Cheyenne Mountain's blast doors are reported to weigh about 25 tons each and to be roughly 3 feet thick, though some sources give 3.5 feet and about 23 tons.
checks.why: Smithsonian Air & Space gives 25 tons and three feet thick, but its excerpt cuts off and other sites give 20-25 tons and about 3.5 feet. No official source was found, so the figures should be hedged.

sources.title: Cheyenne Mountain Complex: The Pinnacle of Security Excellence

checks.claim: About 3 to 4 feet of packed earth (half-value layer roughly 3.6 to 4.8 inches) cuts gamma radiation about 1000-fold, since ten halvings give 2^10 = 1024.
checks.why: A blog gives 3.6 inches per halving and 36 inches for PF1000, but the TACDA civil-defense course says about 40-48 inches is needed. The 3-foot figure holds only with the blog's value, so a range is safer.

sources.title: Nuclear Radiation Shielding Protection and Halving Thickness Values

checks.claim: By the 7-10 rule of thumb, about 49 hours after a blast fallout radiation falls to roughly 1 percent of its level at one hour.
checks.why: Sources describe the rule: each sevenfold increase in time cuts radiation tenfold, so 1 h to 7 h gives 10% and 49 h gives 1%. It is a rule of thumb that assumes fallout of the same effective age.
